newsitem.title: BELGIUM: Belgian growth seen averaging 2.4 pct in 1997 - 2001.
newsitem.headline: Belgian growth seen averaging 2.4 pct in 1997 - 2001.

text.p: Growth in Belgian gross domestic product will be 2.1 percent in 1997, rising to 2.6 percent in 1998 and averaging 2.4 percent a year between 1997 and 2001, the Federal Planning Bureau said on Wednesday.

"It will be driven in the medium term by capital formation and net exports," the Bureau, a government advisory body, said in a statement summarising its annual, five-year rolling economic outlook for the country.
"The rise in private consumption (1.5 percent a year on average) will remain weaker, held back by the relative weakness of real disposable household incomes," it added.

The Planning Bureau said real disposable household incomes would rise by an average of just 1.6 percent a year over the period despite rising employment because the rise in wages would be less than the rise in productivity.
Productivity per head would rise by an average of 1.9 percent a year between 1997 and 2001, it said.
Only about 100,000 jobs would be created during the period.
At the same time the primary surplus, the balance of government spending and revenue excluding debt service costs, would rise from 5.2 percent of GDP in 1996 to six percent in 2001, the Bureau said.
Interest charges on Belgium's 10,000 billion Belgian franc debt would fall from 8.6 percent of GDP in 1996 to 7.1 percent in 2001.

The Belgian government deficit would likewise fall from 3.4 percent of GDP in 1996 to just 1.1 percent in 2001, well below the three percent required for European economic and monetary union (EMU), the Planning Bureau said.

"One can see from this analysis that the risk of exceeding the three percent limit is not eliminated in 1998 and 1999...(but) all risk of exceeding three percent is practically eliminated from 2000," the Bureau said.
